passage: For the landscape and metapopulation analyses, we use \emph{open} boundaries: cells on opposite sides of the grid are not connected. This represents a bounded section of a larger landscape, as in the sampled real landscapes, and allows the same metric definitions to be used for real and simulated data. A forest cluster consists of forest cells connected through this four-neighbour connection rule. We identify forest clusters in Python using the function \texttt{scipy.ndimage.label} (software details are documented in the accompanying project). We call these connected groups forest clusters when describing landscape structure. In the metapopulation model, the same groups represent forest habitat patches, each treated as a local population unit. Their number is $n$, and area $A_i$ is the number of forest cells in group $i$.

Critical distance thresholds provide another perspective on cluster networks. \textcite{Keitt1997CriticalScales} showed that increasing the distance at which clusters are linked can produce an abrupt transition from disconnected groups to a largely connected landscape. This motivates describing the distance needed to connect a specified share of forest. A complementary structural measure is $\mathrm{D50}$, the smallest distance threshold at which the largest connected group of clusters contains at least half of the total forest area. At threshold $d$, clusters $i$ and $j$ are linked when $d_{ij} \leq d$; connections through intermediate clusters also count. If $\mathcal{C}(d)$ denotes the connected components at this threshold and $A_i$ is the area of cluster $i$, then \begin{equation} \mathrm{D50} = \min\left\{d \geq 0 : \frac{\displaystyle\max_{G \in \mathcal{C}(d)} \sum_{i \in G} A_i} {\displaystyle\sum_i A_i} \geq 0.5\right\}. \end{equation} $\mathrm{D50}$ is zero when a single cluster already contains at least half of the forest area. We calculate this threshold using a minimum spanning tree (MST) of the cluster network, adding its edges from shortest to longest. \textcite{UrbanKeitt2001LandscapeConnectivity} established the use of MSTs as compact representations of landscape connectivity. Here, the 50\% forest criterion defines the particular summary used in this thesis. The MST preserves the connected components of the underlying graph at every distance threshold. This metric describes gaps between clusters rather than the dispersal ability of a species. Metric conventions for empty and single-cluster landscapes are documented in the accompanying project.

We selected three bird species to illustrate different empirical response shapes. A descriptive grouping of all 15 empirical curves supported their comparison; its calculation is documented in the accompanying project. For these examples, we also examined how the parameter combinations with the lowest summed errors responded to differences in landscape configuration. For \textit{Lipaugus vociferans}, we additionally checked whether the response persisted among sampled combinations whose summed RMSE was no more than 0.1 above the minimum.

Across all 256 species-parameter combinations, the six analysed landscape metrics showed distinct patterns (Figures~\ref{fig:result-d-median-signed} and~\ref{fig:result-d-connectivity-signed}). Map colours summarise the Spearman correlations between each landscape metric and mean equilibrium patch occupancy. For each parameter combination, they show the median coefficient $r_s$ across forest-cover levels, giving each level equal weight. Values near zero can reflect weak correlations or correlations that change sign as forest cover declines. Additional maps in the accompanying project show how strong the correlations were regardless of their sign, and how consistently they were positive or negative across forest-cover levels.

Figures~\ref{fig:result-d-structure-main-H} and~\ref{fig:result-d-connectivity-main-H} show how the strength and direction of correlations between landscape metrics and occupancy changed as forest cover declined. The median across forest-cover levels used in the maps can hide changes between positive and negative correlations. In region D, for example, both $\chi$ and nearest-neighbour distance changed direction for different forest-cover levels, and $\chi$ became strongly positively associated for landscapes with low forest cover. Many of the intermediate-cover rank relationships were linked to small absolute occupancy differences. The accompanying project therefore also shows results restricted to parameter combinations with an occupancy range of at least 0.05 at each forest-cover level $H$. These additional analyses help assess the size of the underlying response variation but do not resolve the causes of the sign changes.
